I don't know honestly. The documentation does not mention anything about instantiation. The part of  JavaDoc  shared...

> For [Collection](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/6/docs/api/java/util/Collection.html?is-external=true) and Arrays, merging is done by appending incoming data into contents of existing Collection/array

... also could be understood as "incoming collection into existing collection", though the expressions may be ambiguous?
Just because we read and understood JavaDoc this way and implementation works the other way shouldn't mean it's bug --that would be too harsh. Let's wait for @cowtowncoder. We weren't there to help write documentations.

Additionally, here [is blog](https://cowtowncoder.medium.com/jackson-2-9-features-b2a19029e9ff) written about, when @JsonMerge first came out. You may find some more hint on what original intention would be.

I think this case should work so it seems like a legit bug. There are quite a few `@JsonMerge` tests under `com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.deser.merge`, including `CollectionMergeTest`. But I suspect none tests custom `List` for which deserializer can't be created -- so you may have uncovered an edge case @nlisker .

Checking in simplified/minimal reproduction under `src/test/java/.../tofix` would make sense.

body:
Okay, going through the reproduction over and over, got me wondering... How would Mapper would update existing list if there is no shared connection between the original object and deserialization? The list field is not and cannot even be static 🤔

So I went on to read a [Baeldung blog](https://www.baeldung.com/java-jsonmerge-annotation-jackson) written about `@JsonMerge` usage.  And using that proper usage, test passes.

We should be doing like ...

     MAPPER.readerForUpdating(Object).readValue(("{\"values\":[\"x\"]}"), MergeList.class);`

... this, where as original reproduction was only using....

    `MAPPER.readValue(("{\"values\":[\"x\"]}"), MergeList.class);` 

I wrote a test PR #4784 to demonstrate that, @nlisker so PTAL.

@nlisker I think the problem really is that construction of deserializer for custom type fails due to it being abstract type -- and we do need a `JsonDeserializer` to actually do merge (it's part of `deserialize()` that is given existing value to modify).
To fix this, we'd need to figure out how to postpone failure due to lack of Creator (it's abstract type...).
In theory this is doable, of course, but in practice many things are done eagerly and are difficult to change to do on-demand (and more complex, less efficient). The thing is: code that looks up `JsonDeserializer` does not (and maybe cannot) know that `ValueInstantiator` is not needed -- it simply does not have that information.

In the meantime, you might be able to work around the issue if you can use concrete type instead of `MyList`. Or possible having static factory method annotated with `@JsonCreator` on it (it need not to anything, won't be called on merge case).
I mention this because actual fix may be difficult to figure out.

So basically: `List`/`Collection` are mapped to defaults (some well-known types, like `ArrayList`), and they all are concrete, have 0-args constructor, so it's known how to construct instances (to create `ValueInstantiator`). As such, deserializer can be created.
This is not true for `MyList`.

@JooHyukKim I think your `MyArrayList` work because it is concrete type with no-args Constructor.

But I am not 100% sure if (and if so, why) `mapper.readerForUpdating()` might work around the isssue -- there would still be need for deserializer in that case.

@nlisker Oh. Another thing that would work is a custom `JsonDeserializer` for `MyList` (registered via Module or `@JsonDeserialize(using = ...)` annotation). That'd need to implement merging by overloading secondary `deserialize()` method (one taking existing value). Not sure how easy it'd be use `CollectionDeserializer` (or one of base classes).

There's already a workaround with a custom setter that I wrote in the initial post.

I don't understand why a deserializer is needed for an instance that is already created. As can be seen in the setter workaround, Jackson already knows to create a `List` as an input to the setter (or `Map` if I have a custom map). From there it's a matter of abiding by the contract of `List`. What am I missing?
